archetype.name: Fringe Contender (pass-first, pass-rush revival)
archetype.definition: A Burrow-driven, pass-heavy team whose defense has jumped from bottom-tier to top-10 by EPA, good enough to make the playoffs but not yet proven against good offenses.

report.headline: Passing game is heating up, but the defensive leap was built against soft offenses
report.take:
Cincinnati is a quarterback team that knows it. The Bengals throw more than any team relative to situation (pass rate over expected +7.2, 1st) because the run game gives them little: 3.57 yards per carry and a rush EPA of -0.104, 18th. Burrow has started every game and thrown for 1,171 yards, about 293 a game, with Tee Higgins (39 targets) and Ja'Marr Chase (28) as the main options and Chase Brown (24) as the outlet. The offense ranks 10th in EPA. The league is used to that from them. The defense is what has changed.

The defense is the story. From 2023 to 2025 this unit ranked 28th, 27th and 29th in EPA allowed. Last year it gave up 28.9 points a game. Now it sits 10th, and the pass rush is doing it: 14 sacks (3rd), an 8.7% sack rate (2nd) and a 24.2% pressure rate (7th). Without that rush the 2-2 record would look much worse.

The record hides a lot in both directions. The Week 1 win over Tampa came with negative passing EPA (-2.6) and was rescued by four takeaways. The two losses came in Burrow's two best passing games (+14.7 at Pittsburgh, +7.4 against Jacksonville, including 428 yards). They were lost to two turnovers each, zero or one takeaway, a vanishing run game (23 rushing yards vs JAX) and 108 penalty yards in Week 4. The defensive numbers also carry a schedule caveat. Three of the four offenses faced now rank 20th, 25th and 32nd in EPA. The one good offense, Jacksonville at 7th, scored 22 points. The unit also ranks 23rd in yards allowed, 23rd on third downs, 30th in missed tackles and 30th against short passes. A 30.8% red-zone TD rate allowed (3rd) is holding the scoreboard together, and that rate rarely stays this low.

The direction is still positive. Point differential is +3 a game (10th), net EPA ranks 12th, and wins over expected sit at -0.26, so the record is not inflated. The passing game is trending up, and the next two games before the bye stretch are Miami and Tennessee, both 0-4. The cap on this team is whether the rush holds up once offenses like Baltimore and Kansas City show up. The immediate question is whether Chase (concussion) and Higgins (groin) are on the field.

strengths.title: A pass rush that finishes
strengths.body: Cincinnati is converting pressure into sacks at an elite rate: a top-seven pressure rate turned into the league's second-best sack rate. It has produced at least two sacks every week and four in three of four games. Sack rates are noisier than pressure rates, so some cooling is likely. Still, the pressure baseline is good enough to keep this a real strength.

strengths.title: Burrow's passing game is rounding into form
strengths.body: After two sluggish weeks, the passing offense produced +14.7 and +7.4 EPA in Weeks 3 and 4, including a 428-yard day. The volume is built in because the staff leans on the pass harder than anyone. That holds as long as the top two receivers are healthy.

strengths.title: Red-zone and short-yardage execution
strengths.body: The defense has allowed touchdowns on just 30.8% of red-zone trips, and the offense converts 85.7% of short-yardage tries (4th) despite a poor run game overall. Short-yardage conversion reflects a real scheme and line skill. The red-zone defense number is the more fragile of the two.

concerns.title: Bend-don't-break defense likely to bend more
concerns.body: Behind the good EPA ranking sit 348.8 yards allowed a game (23rd), a 44% third-down rate allowed (23rd), the 30th-ranked short-pass defense and the 30th-ranked missed-tackle rate. Those are the habits that keep drives alive. The red-zone stops covering for them will likely regress. The numbers also came mostly against weak offenses, and the secondary is now missing S Bryan Cook and CB Jalen Davis (IR).

concerns.title: Self-inflicted damage: penalties and giveaways
concerns.body: Nine penalties a game ranks 27th, with 4.3 on the line alone. The 108 penalty yards against Jacksonville were part of why a 428-yard passing day produced 17 points. Four giveaways in the two losses turned efficient offense into defeats. This is a discipline problem more than a talent one, which makes it fixable, but it has not been fixed yet.

concerns.title: No run game, Burrow taking hits
concerns.body: The run game is below average almost across the board, bottoming out at 23 yards against Jacksonville. That makes the offense one-dimensional. Burrow has absorbed 32 QB hits (31st) despite one of the quickest release profiles in the league, and he took five sacks at Houston. A heavy dropback load behind this protection is the season's biggest risk.

trend.note: The results have run W, W, L, L while the passing EPA has gone the other way (-2.6, -0.5, +14.7, +7.4). The early wins leaned on takeaways (four in Week 1) and the losses on giveaways and penalties. The underlying offense is improving even as the record slides.

nextGame.headline: Bengals' pass rush meets the league's weakest team on the road
nextGame.body:
Miami ranks last in net EPA and last in scoring at 11.5 points a game. Its profile fits what Cincinnati does well. The Dolphins' pass defense ranks 29th in EPA allowed and generates the third-lowest pressure rate (12.1%), so Burrow should have clean pockets and big windows. Their run defense is solid (9th), which matters little to a team that throws this much anyway. On the other side, Malik Willis is behind a line allowing an 8.7% sack rate while holding the ball a long time, in a run-first offense whose rushing EPA ranks 28th. That is a good setup for the Bengals' rush.

Availability swings this game. Higgins (groin, day-to-day) and Chase (concussion, left the Jacksonville game) are both questionable. Without them the targets fall to Brown, Dohnte Meyers and Mike Gesicki, and the -7 looks less comfortable. The Bengals defense is short S Bryan Cook, S Kyle Dugger, DT B.J. Hill and CB Jalen Davis. Miami's injuries hit harder: De'Von Achane is on IR with a torn ACL, top receiver Caleb Douglas (89% of snaps) is out, two cornerbacks are out, and S Dante Trader Jr. is questionable. That further thins a pass defense that is already leaking.

keyMatchups.title: Bengals rush vs Miami's leaky protection
keyMatchups.body: Cincinnati has the league's second-best sack rate. Miami's line allows a 27th-ranked sack rate and a 29th-ranked pressure rate. Willis holding the ball against this front is the clearest mismatch on the field, and drive-killing sacks should keep Miami's scoring low.

keyMatchups.title: Burrow vs a soft, short-handed secondary
keyMatchups.body: Miami allows +0.276 EPA per dropback (29th) and barely pressures the quarterback. Now it is missing cornerbacks Reese Taylor and Storm Duck. Even with backup receivers, Cincinnati's pass-first approach lines up with Miami's biggest weakness. Miami's 64.7% red-zone TD rate allowed means drives should end in touchdowns rather than field goals.

keyMatchups.title: Miami's run game without Achane
keyMatchups.body: The Dolphins run more than the situation calls for (-9.4 pass rate over expected) even though their rushing ranks 28th in EPA, and now their lead back is out for the year. Cincinnati has allowed explosive runs at a 25th-ranked rate, so a few chunk gains are possible. Sustained drives are unlikely.

nextGame.watch: Whether Chase and Higgins are active. Healthy, this is a mismatch. Without both, Cincinnati's thin run game has to carry more than it can against a top-10 run defense.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense should stay a top-12 unit as long as Burrow and the top two receivers are upright. Weeks 3 and 4 look more like its real level than Weeks 1 and 2. Expect the defense to drift down from 10th as the red-zone luck fades and the schedule adds Baltimore twice and Kansas City. That said, a defense with this pass rush is not the 2025 group that ranked 29th. The schedule splits cleanly. Miami, Tennessee, Washington, New Orleans and Indianapolis are games a top-12 team should win more often than not. The six games against BAL, CLE (twice each), PIT and KC will decide the division.

The record sits right where the point differential says it should, so there is no regression owed in either direction. Fewer penalties and a turnover margin closer to the passing game's efficiency would push this into the 10-win range. More hits on Burrow is the scenario that sinks it.
swingFactors: Whether the pass rush holds up against BAL and KC

bets.reason: Miami averages 11.5 points (32nd) and has lost its lead back and top receiver. It now faces the league's second-best sack rate behind a line that ranks 27th at preventing sacks.
Miami's games average 36.8 combined points (11.5 scored + 25.3 allowed). A Dolphins offense this limited caps the total. The risk is a Bengals passing explosion against a soft secondary.

The net EPA gap is enormous (+0.069 vs -0.236), and Miami is 1-3 against the spread with a -13.8 point differential. Treat this as conditional on Chase or Higgins playing. Cincinnati's penalties and giveaways have kept its margins tight.

Cincinnati has 3.5 sacks a game and has reached four in three of four weeks. Miami allows an 8.7% sack rate with long times to throw. Willis's run-heavy usage trims dropbacks, which keeps this a lean.

confidence.note: Only four games, mostly against weak offenses, and the top two receivers are questionable.
